doc.title: Steve Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 25, 2002

title: Jazz education and the oral tradition
summary: Musicians joining education, but the oral tradition and folk core of the music matter.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: We had mentioned the IAJE thing and it seems like it’s almost a necessity these days for jazz musicians to get involved in the education scene.

Yeah. Yeah I think fortunately, now I’ve seen the trend in the last ten years where more of the street musicians have gotten involved, musicians that are in the scene, of the scene, in addition to educators. And I think that’s been a positive. I think Bunky Green had a lot to do with that when he was president, to get a lot of the musicians involved. Of course I know that even before that there was — you had guys like Kenny Barron and Larry

Ridley who were teaching at Rutgers and then you had Rufus Reid who was head of the program at William Paterson for many years and recently retired. So there has always been that factor involved. But in the more recent times we’ve seen a big influx of that. And I hope that turns out to be a positive. Because again, education is good. But without the oral tradition, to get the unteachable nuances so to speak of the music, the spiritual elements of the music, there’s nothing like the oral tradition. There’s nothing like taking a younger musician aside and saying hey you know what? Instead of doing it like that, think about it like this. Instead of counting in four-four, count in two-two, which is another thing I learned from Lionel Hampton. So all of those little things, and talking about the experiences that we’ve all had with each other, that’s important in the development of young musicians. And we can’t — the music cannot go forward without that. There are different ways to disseminate the information. We can always learn about chord changes about theory, which is great and I think it’s necessary to be a professional working musician these days. But those other things, those other intangibles, it’s always what made this music what it is. It is at its core and at its root, it’s a folk music. This is really folk music first and foremost, and will always be. That’s its greatness, that’s part of its greatness. And I think any great music draws from that. So we can’t lose it.
